methodist.sanctification:
Methodists follow John Wesley in teaching that the Christian life is meant to grow in holiness, a journey which Wesley called going on to perfection. Christian perfection means perfect love: loving God with all the heart and loving one's neighbor as oneself. It is not a claim to be free of mistakes, weakness or ignorance, and it is a gift of God's grace received by faith, not an achievement.

Methodists differ in how they understand this. Some, especially in Wesleyan and Holiness bodies, expect a definite moment of entire sanctification, while others emphasize gradual growth throughout life. The common conviction is that God's grace does more than forgive, that it truly transforms, and that believers should expect and pray for real growth in holiness and love.
methodist.predestination:
Methodists teach that God's grace goes before us, and call this prevenient grace: God is at work in every person before they respond, awakening conscience and enabling them to hear the gospel and to answer freely. God desires all people to be saved, and Christ died for all.

For this reason Methodists do not hold to unconditional election, the teaching that God chooses some individuals for salvation and passes over the rest. They speak instead of a conditional election, in which God's foreknowledge sees who will respond in faith, and grace makes the response possible without forcing it. They distinguish their view from the Reformed teaching, and they say that human responsibility and God's grace both matter.
methodist.perseverance:
Methodists teach that a Christian can fall from grace. Salvation is a real relationship with God, and a person who has received it can turn away through persistent unbelief or willful sin and lose it. This is why Scripture contains warnings addressed to believers, and why Methodists take them seriously.

They do not teach that the fall is easy or the norm. They stress that God is faithful, that believers can have a real assurance of his love, and that the Holy Spirit keeps those who trust in Christ. A person who has fallen away may return through repentance, since God's mercy remains open. They differ here from traditions which hold that the truly saved cannot finally be lost.
methodist.means_of_grace:
Methodists speak of the means of grace: the ordinary channels through which God gives his grace to his people. Following John Wesley, they name works of piety such as prayer, reading and hearing Scripture, the Lord's Supper, fasting and Christian fellowship, as well as works of mercy such as caring for the poor and the sick.

None of these earns salvation, but each is a place where God meets us and strengthens faith and love. Methodists stress that they should be practiced regularly and in community, and Wesley urged frequent participation in the Lord's Supper. The class meeting, small groups for mutual accountability and encouragement, was another means that gave early Methodism its character, and many congregations still value small groups.
methodist.free_will:
Methodists believe that human beings can freely respond to God, and that they are responsible for their answer. Because of the effects of sin, this freedom does not come by nature. It is restored by God's prevenient grace, which goes before and enables every person to accept or to resist the offer of salvation.

This means that faith is a real human act, and also a gift made possible by God, so that no one can boast. It also means that God does not force anyone, and that people can refuse. Methodists distinguish their view from teaching that God's choice alone decides, and from views in which people can save themselves. They understand free will as grace-enabled and always dependent on God.
methodist.episcopacy:
In many Methodist bodies, including the United Methodist Church and the African Methodist Episcopal churches, bishops provide oversight. They preside over annual conferences or regions, ordain clergy, and appoint pastors to their congregations, and they are elected and consecrated for this ministry.

Methodists describe the office as a form of service and leadership and not as a claim to an unbroken succession from the apostles through a line of ordinations. In the United Methodist Church a bishop is understood to be an elder who is set apart for oversight, and not a separate order of ministry. The exact arrangements, such as terms of office and how bishops are chosen, differ among Methodist denominations.
methodist.ordination_of_women:
Most Methodist churches ordain women as pastors and elders, and many have women bishops. In the Methodist tradition the call to ministry is understood as coming from God through gifts, grace and fruit, and the church's role is to test and affirm the call, whoever receives it. John Wesley himself accepted women as preachers when he saw evidence of their gifts.

In the United Methodist tradition, women have been granted full clergy rights since the middle of the twentieth century. Some smaller and more conservative Wesleyan bodies differ, and members can hold varying personal views. In general, Methodists see women's ordination as a natural outgrowth of the belief that God's grace is offered to all and that all may be called to serve.
